feed.title: The Peters Lab
feed.subtitle: The Peters Lab at the University of Richmond studies how memories are formed. We use single-particle cryo-electron microscopy, computational structural biology, and cell imaging to reveal the molecular machinery that strengthens synapses during long-term potentiation.

entry.title: Undergraduate researchers, Chris Carr and Rain Tela, honored with departmental awards

link.title: Undergraduate researchers, Chris Carr and Rain Tela, honored with departmental awards

entry.content:
Rain Tela (left) and Chris Carr (right) were each recognized with departmental awards for the 2025-2026 academic year.

Rain was awarded the Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Junior Research Award, which is given to a BMB major with outstanding research performance and dedication. Rain was honored for her tenacity and progress in research.

Chris was awarded the Clarence Denoon Award, which is given to a rising senior for excellence in the natural sciences. Chris was awarded due to his progress in lab as well as his outstanding performance in the classroom.

entry.title: Perspective: Getting students excited about introductory biology

link.title: Perspective: Getting students excited about introductory biology

entry.content:
I am excited to share a recent perspective piece I wrote, entitled Getting students excited about introductory biology for ASBMB Today.

In this piece, I discuss how I’ve used an opioids case study to teach introductory cell and molecular biology.

I am a big fan of case studies, and I’m happy to chat with anyone interested in learning more!

entry.title: Publication: Designing life science assessments in the era of generative artificial intelligence

link.title: Publication: Designing life science assessments in the era of generative artificial intelligence

entry.content:
I am excited to share a new paper published in PLOS ONE from the education side of the lab.

There is a lot of anxiety that genAI tools will jeopardize learning gains from homework assignments. Using Bloom’s Taxonomy, we analyzed where genAI succeeds and where it struggles.

We compared the performance of ChatGPT-4o and Harvard PhD students in designing molecular biology experiments. Initially, we predicted that as you move higher in Bloom’s Taxonomy, ChatGPT would perform worse. However, that is not what we observed.

The main difference we observed in performance was at the “apply” level of Bloom’s. While students (mean = 87%) performed two letter grades better than ChatGPT (mean = 67%) on experimental design worksheets, all of that difference can be explained by a difference in performance at the “apply” level. We posit that apply-level questions require multi-step, compositional reasoning, which large language models are not well-suited for. Therefore, this finding is likely broadly applicable across LLMs.

At the “create” level, genAI consistently generated reasonable hypotheses for given scenarios. However, the hypotheses often lacked the specificity and testability we would expect of PhD-level work.

We also observed that ChatGPT-4o struggled to interpret data presented graphically. Anecdotally, ChatGPT-5.4-Thinking has dramatically improved at data interpretation. This is one of many examples emphasizing how educators must be mindful of the rapidly developing genAI landscape.

We offer a few suggestions to educators. One that I’ve used in my teaching is increasing my expectation for precision in students’ answers. GenAI is great at producing reasonable-sounding answers, but precision can be lacking. Use rubrics that reward careful justification for answers.

The class we describe in the paper uses “chalk talks” as a key assessment. Oral exams are valuable assessment tools that maximize student ownership of their answers. The class is also an example of a “flipped classroom,” which gives frequent opportunities for formative assessments.

All in all, many examples of “good” pedagogy (e.g., active learning, flipped classrooms, universal design) are also beneficial for maintaining learning gains in the era of genAI.
entry.summary: I am excited to share a new paper published in PLOS ONE from the education side of the lab.

entry.title: Undergraduate researchers, Chris Carr and Kalynn Cheeks, honored with departmental awards

link.title: Undergraduate researchers, Chris Carr and Kalynn Cheeks, honored with departmental awards

entry.content:
Kalynn Cheeks (left) and Chris Carr (right) were each recognized with departmental awards for the 2024-2025 academic year.

Kalynn was awarded the Willie M. Reams Award for Outstanding Achievement, one of the Biology Department’s highest honors. Kalynn was honored for her research efforts in the Richardson Lab, her outstanding performance in the classroom, and her contributions to the Peters Lab.

Chris was awarded the Biochemistry and Molecular Biology Sophomore Research Award. Chris was honored for his outstanding potential to perform research, based on his progress so far in the Peters Lab.

Congratulations to both Chris and Kalynn!
entry.summary: Kalynn Cheeks (left) and Chris Carr (right) were each recognized with departmental awards for the 2024-2025 academic year.

entry.title: Peters Lab is Awarded National Science Foundation Grant

link.title: Peters Lab is Awarded National Science Foundation Grant

entry.content:
The Peters Lab received a $502,981 award from the National Science Foundation to explore the basic mechanisms of memory formation.

The grant will be used to:

  • Purchase equipment and tools
  • Hire a research technician
  • Fund undergraduate research
  • Fund undergraduate travel to conferences and national laboratories

In addition, the grant provides support for the creation of a new course at the University of Richmond in advanced molecular biology.

Altogether, this grant will help train the next generation of scientists in America and will contribute to our understanding of how memories form.
entry.summary: The Peters Lab received a $502,981 award from the National Science Foundation to explore the basic mechanisms of memory formation.
